questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I could choose between Madrid, Cáceres, Barcelona or Salamanca. I went with the place that i already hadn't been to and which wasn't a metropolitan big city. That is, i went with Salamanca. Moreover, I like to explore new places without looking into them beforehand and so I thought Salamanca would be a fun experience in that regard since it is more or less unknown to the common man outside of Spain. Also i got to study philosophy which i had gotten a taste for up until that point, considering it was a requirement for going there, and so i thought 'Let's goooo'. Why not. Let's try something new. What is the worst that could happen?

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The spanish system of education is what i would call in my common tongue a "rodebutik". Would not recommend going there for educational purposes since the bureaucracy is what sailors in time past memorial called drowning 'like going home'.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I don't recall there being any special information that i needed to know upon getting there. That being said, it as quite easy finding my way as long as one can ask for directions and so forth so there is that.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I don't recall there being any assitance at all.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There is basically none, but that is fine. I expected it and found my own way.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Incredibly difficult since almost every landlord in the city only rented out his/her accomodation for the entire year and not only for the semester which is what i was looking for. I only found a place at the last moment possible at an expensive price and heard from several other on erasmus there who had to sign contracts for the whole year even though they only stayed for a single semester.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: They should know that a good roomate is more valuable than any good acommodation. Find a good roommate is more important than the apartment.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It is like the last time i went on exchange with erasmus. There is a lot of unnecessary bureaucracy going back and forth between institutions, signing, expressing that 'yes, i comply to the rules' and so forth. So i knew what i was going into.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I don't recall there being any. Although, there might have been some available, but as i recall it i think it was more catered towards students of bachelors degrees.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was successfull, although, and i thought this being there for the first weeks getting a feeling for the classes, there is no way that i would be able to choose any other classes, since the registration process for getting the classes approved is incredibly cumbersome and slow. The option is obviously there, but before getting through with the process of actually getting them registered so that one can get access to the host university's webpage before being halfway through the semester is just not a realistic proposition.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Choose carefully the classes that you want to pick because there is no time to change them one you get there. The system is simply too rigid. And make sure also that you make sure your classes are within a certain timeframe one from the other during the day. That is, don't choose classes in the morning and in the afternoon on the same day.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Competent teachers obviously, but the overall level of the academic programme was brought down by a cumbersome rigid system that is impossible to follow. That is, the programme is chaoticly put together, or at least so was the ones i chose. For an example, i had 6 small courses at 3 ECTS each, those courses each were then SUBDIVIDED into smaller sessions, for an example directed by 3 different teachers over several weeks intermingled with other courses. 
This ended up in me actually missing an exam because i was handed a portfolio document not knowing it was an actual exam that needed to be handed in since the course and the examination document had diferent titles.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Veyr different since every teacher has his own style. Some used the intranet for giving out homework, other only in hand. Some used the chalkboard for teaching, some just taught with a monologue and others used PP as well.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
"Filosofía del Lenguaje I", although i would only recommend it if the student has a passion for linguistics with an aptitude for mathematics as well (of which i didn't). The teacher is great and the subject very interesting if you were to dive into subjects beyond the grammar of languages. 
"Historia de la Estética y de la Teoría de las Artes". Interesting subject that for our part delved into the philosophy behind how art and aesthetics is/could be perceived. Good teacher as well, although a little finecky and controlling at times.
"-Historia de la Filosofía Moderna y Contemporánea", had a good selection of teachers that all seemed quite competent and engaging in each their own subject. Interesting chats.

questions.answer: housing was more expensive than anticipated

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: housing was more expensive, food was less expensive. Also going out for eating is many times a better deal than buying groceries in the supermarket.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There were quite a bit, but the majority from what i could see were for bachelor students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Find local people to hang out with. Especially if you would like to learn the language. In that sense i would actually abstain from going to erasmus events and rather i would mingle with the locals. But that is just my recommendation.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: There is a beautiful mountain range just south of Salamanca which is beautiful for walking and seing small towns. Garganta la olla is one.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy if you find some local friends.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Yea, go to outdoor traning sites. Create a community and go from there. That's what i did. I made a ton of local friends (only spaniards and latin americans) with whom i could practice my spanish. Perfect.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not that many actually, other than what i already described with the difference to academic processes.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The warmth of the spanish people is second to none. They invite you straight into their hearts and become your friend easily. Likewise with many latin americans

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Only go if you truly want to go. DO NOT, like i did, choose hard courses, for the love of god. Don't choose philosophy if you already havn't finished a bachelors in philosophy. Otherwise you will not only get frustrated by the high level of spanish, which is inevitable - your level is going to be far lower than  that of the natives obviously, but also by the fact that you have no experience with philosophy and so everything is going to feel overwhelming and you won't be able to understand anything going on.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Information about accomodation in Salamanca would be useful information and also if the student is an L2 student studying languages how difficult it is to accostum to philosophy.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know a lot of amazing people. And also, even though it wasn't the best experience, getting to know more about philosophy in general

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Being a L2 student of spanish combined with studying master level philosophy being a novice myself in the subject.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
